notes.meaning: This message came about a month after the people had started work on the temple again. The date fell during the Feast of Tabernacles, a happy harvest festival, but the harvest had been poor. God sent words of comfort to the same leaders and people who had just obeyed him. Those who are hearty in God's work get fresh encouragement from him.

Solomon's temple had been destroyed about seventy years earlier, so some old people still remembered it. Next to that grand building, the new one looked like nothing, and some of them wept (Ezra 3:12). Their sad comparisons made the builders lose heart. But God judges things differently than people do.

God tells the governor, the high priest and all the people to take heart and keep working. They should do as well as they can, even if they cannot do as well as they would like. Their strength is that the LORD of Hosts is with them. When God gives a command, he also gives the help to obey it.

God reminds them of his covenant, the binding promise he made when he brought Israel out of Egypt. That promise still stands. His Spirit is still among them to strengthen them, so they need not be afraid.

God once shook the earth at Mount Sinai when he gave the law. Now he promises a greater shaking of heaven, earth, sea and land. Hebrews 12:26 applies this to the coming of Christ's kingdom, which cannot be shaken. Many see it begun at Christ's first coming and finished at his second.

God will shake all the nations. Older English Bibles read, "the desire of all nations shall come." Many older commentators take this to mean Christ, the one the nations truly long for. God would fill this temple with glory when Christ came and taught in it.

differ.view: Some read the phrase as the nations' treasures, as the BSB does. They believe God will move the nations to bring their riches to honor his house.

notes.meaning: All the silver and gold in the world already belongs to God. So the people need not worry that this temple has less gold than Solomon's did. God could supply gold if he wished, but he plans a far better glory. If we have money, we should honor God with it; if not, he accepts what we have.

The new temple never matched Solomon's in outward beauty. Its greater glory came from the presence of the Messiah, who was brought there as a baby and later taught in it. The promised peace is mainly the peace with God that Jesus bought with his blood. That peace then fills the heart.
This new message came two months later, around December. By then the winter crops had been sown, and the people had made good progress on the building.
Haggai was a prophet, but he was told to ask the priests about God's law. Their job was to explain it. Haggai respected their role, and their own answers would help him make his point.

Meat from a sacrifice was holy, and it made the cloth that carried it holy. But that holiness could not pass on to other food the cloth touched. The priests rightly answered no. Holy things do not make other things holy just by touching them.

A person who touched a dead body became unclean, and whatever he touched became unclean too (Numbers 19:22). The priests rightly answered yes. Uncleanness spreads more easily than holiness. As one writer put it, a drop of filth spoils clean water, but drops of clean water will not clean a pot of filth.

God applies the lesson to the people. While they neglected his house, they were like the unclean man, and even their sacrifices on the altar were unclean. God calls them "this people," not "my people." Good works and offerings please God only when they come from a heart that is right with him.

God asks them to think back to the time before they started building. A farmer expected twenty measures of grain from a heap but found only ten. At the winepress he expected fifty measures but got only twenty. Their harvests kept coming up short.

God himself sent scorching winds, mildew and hail on their crops. These words echo Amos 4:9. God meant these troubles to call them back, but they did not turn to him. They blamed chance or did not see their own sin.
Now God asks them to look forward from this very day. On this day they began building in earnest on the foundation laid years before. God wants them to notice how things change from here on.

The seed was in the ground, and the fruit trees had not yet borne anything. Nothing yet showed whether there would be a good harvest. But God promised, "From this day on I will bless you." When the plenty came, it would be clear that it came from God. We can trust his promise even before we see any sign of it.
On the same day, God gave Haggai a second message. This one was just for Zerubbabel, the governor. He led the work and carried the cares of the whole nation.

God repeats that he will shake heaven and earth. He will bring down proud kingdoms and their armies, and they will even destroy one another. The small, weak nation need not fear these upheavals. This also points to Christ's kingdom, which will overcome every power that opposes it (Daniel 2:44).

A signet ring was a king's seal ring. It was precious, always kept close, and used to show his authority. God had said he would pull King Jeconiah off like a signet ring (Jeremiah 22:24). Now he makes Zerubbabel, Jeconiah's descendant, his precious ring, by his own free choice and not because Zerubbabel earned it. This was never fully true of Zerubbabel himself. It points to Jesus, born from Zerubbabel's family line, who holds all authority from the Father.
